source.text: Yongjia Xuanjue, Song of Realizing the Way (Taishō T2014): 15 passages selected from its 247 lines, in their original order
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

jd01.heading: The Leisurely Person of the Way
jd01.plain: Have you not seen? The leisurely person of the Way, beyond learning and with nothing to do, neither tries to remove deluded thoughts nor seeks the truth. The true nature of ignorance is Buddha-nature; this illusory, empty body is the Dharma body.
jd01.commentary: The opening of the Song. The awakened one does not discard delusion and wander in search of truth, because there is no ignorance to throw away apart from a Buddha-nature to seek. The first line holds the heart of Seon: this very body and mind are the Buddha's body.

jd02.heading: The Dharma Body Without a Single Thing
jd02.plain: When you awaken to the Dharma body, there is not a single thing; the original source, your own nature, is the Buddha just as it is. The five aggregates drift idly back and forth like floating clouds; the three poisons rise and vanish in vain like bubbles on water.
jd02.commentary: Body and mind (the five aggregates) and greed, anger and delusion (the three poisons) have no substance, like clouds and bubbles. Though they come and go, the original nature is not stained.

jd03.heading: When True Reality Is Realized
jd03.plain: When true reality is realized, there is neither self nor dharmas, and the karma that leads to the Avīci hell vanishes in an instant. If these were lies to deceive beings, I would bring upon myself the punishment of having my tongue torn out for kalpas as many as dust and sand.
jd03.commentary: Speaking of the power of awakening, he stakes his life on his words. The oath that he would go to the hell of tongue-tearing if he lied declares that this song is truth born of experience.

jd04.heading: In the Dream and After Waking
jd04.plain: Once you suddenly awaken to the Tathāgata's Seon, the six pāramitās and all practices are perfectly complete in its substance. In the dream the six realms were vivid and clear; after waking, all is empty, and there is not even the great universe.
jd04.commentary: "In the dream they were clearly there; after waking all is empty" is one of the most quoted lines of the Song. With the eye of awakening it sings that the world of saṃsāra is like an empty dream.

jd05.heading: The Dusty Mirror
jd05.plain: There is no wrong and no blessing, no loss and no gain; in the nature of stillness and extinction, do not ask or seek. Until now the dusty mirror has never been polished; today it must be clearly cut open and made bright.
jd05.commentary: In the original nature there is not even a distinction between wrongs and blessings, but a mind that has lived without knowing this is like a dusty mirror. It urges us to polish that mirror today.

jd06.heading: Ask the Wooden Puppet
jd06.plain: Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If there is truly no birth, there is no non-birth either. Call the wooden puppet worked by strings and ask it: if you strive to seek the Buddha, when will you ever succeed?
jd06.commentary: Seeking non-birth by cutting off thought is just another attachment. It is a sharp rebuke: trying to become a Buddha by contrivance, like a wooden puppet, will never succeed.

jd07.heading: Let Go of the Four Elements
jd07.plain: Let go of the four elements that make up the body and do not grasp them. Within the still nature, simply drink and eat as you go. All conditioned things are impermanent and everything is empty: this is the Tathāgata's great, perfect awakening.
jd07.commentary: It tells us not to cling to the body, and to live ordinary life, eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, just as the still nature. Realizing impermanence and emptiness is awakening itself.

jd08.heading: Cut Straight to the Root
jd08.plain: With certain words I reveal the true practitioner; if anyone does not believe, let them question as they like. Cutting straight to the root is what the Buddha sealed; plucking leaves and searching branches I do not know how to do.
jd08.commentary: Clinging to words and theories and wandering among them is chasing leaves and branches. This declares that Seon is the way of seeing the root of the mind directly.

jd09.heading: The Maṇi Jewel
jd09.plain: People do not recognize the maṇi jewel, but it is personally gathered within the Tathāgatagarbha. The six wondrous functions are empty yet not empty; the single round light is form yet not form.
jd09.commentary: Everyone carries a priceless jewel (Buddha-nature) within but does not recognize it. The workings of the six senses, seeing, hearing and feeling, are that jewel's light.

jd10.heading: The Moon in the Water
jd10.plain: Purifying the five eyes and gaining the five powers can only be known by awakening; it is hard to reckon. Seeing a form in a mirror is not hard, but how can you scoop up the moon in the water by hand?
jd10.commentary: Awakening is not known by reckoning with the head. As the moon reflected in water cannot be caught by hand, trying to grasp it with thought misses it.

jd11.heading: Always Walking Alone
jd11.plain: Always going alone, always walking alone, yet those who have arrived wander together on the road of nirvana. The tune is ancient, the spirit clear, the bearing naturally lofty; the face is gaunt and the bones upright, and people do not give a second look.
jd11.commentary: The practitioner walking alone resembles the "rhinoceros horn" of the Sutta Nipāta. Though their outward appearance is humble, the awakened are all companions on the same road.

jd12.heading: The Poor Practitioner
jd12.plain: The poor disciple of the Buddha says with the mouth that they are poor, but in truth only the body is poor; the Way is not poor. Being poor, the body always wears a patched robe; having the Way, the heart holds a priceless treasure.
jd12.commentary: It sings of the dignity of a practitioner who owns nothing. Though the body wears rags, the heart holds a treasure that nothing in the world could buy.

jd13.heading: Walking Is Seon, Sitting Is Seon
jd13.plain: Walking is Seon, sitting is Seon; in speaking and silence, moving and stillness, the essence is at peace. Even meeting the blade of a sword, one is always calm; even made to drink poison, one is at ease.
jd13.commentary: "Walking is Seon, sitting is Seon" is a famous line showing that Seon is not only in seated meditation but in every moment of life. A mind unshaken before any danger is the power of Seon.

jd14.heading: One Moon in All Waters
jd14.plain: One nature pervades all natures; one dharma contains all dharmas. One moon appears in all waters; all the moons in the waters are gathered into one moon.
jd14.commentary: There is one moon in the sky, yet a thousand rivers reflect a thousand moons. This famous line sings, with the image of moon and water, of the Avataṃsaka world where the one and the whole contain each other. The title of King Sejong's Songs of the Moon's Reflection on a Thousand Rivers comes from this image.

jd15.heading: Marks on the Mirror
jd15.plain: Mind is the root and dharmas are the dust; the two are like marks on a mirror. Only when the marks and grime are all gone does the light begin to show; when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, the nature is true.
jd15.commentary: The seeing mind and the objects seen are both like smudges on a mirror. When both are laid down, the original bright light shows.

dharmakaya.definition: The Buddha's body as truth itself, without form, birth or death, pervading the whole universe.

avidya.definition: The root delusion of not knowing the true nature of things.

skandha.definition: The five heaps that make up body and mind: form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness.

three-poisons.definition: The three poisons that harm the mind: greed, anger and delusion.

avici.definition: The gravest hell, where suffering continues without interruption; the uninterrupted hell.

six-paramitas.definition: The six practices of a bodhisattva: giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and wisdom.

six-paths.definition: The six worlds beings cycle through in birth and death: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans and heavenly beings.

four-elements.definition: The four elements that make up the body and matter: earth, water, fire and wind.

anicca.definition: The truth that everything conditioned is always changing and never stays. One of the three marks of existence.

mani.definition: A wish-fulfilling jewel said to grant whatever one wishes; an image for the Buddha-nature everyone has.

tathagatagarbha.definition: The Tathāgata's nature hidden within all beings: only covered by afflictions, originally pure.

nirvana.definition: The stillness in which the fires of greed, anger and delusion have gone out.
